summary:
The Earth Jukebox is a web application that lets anyone hear how our planet is changing. We developed an interface that pairs visual frames from NASA’s Earth Information Center with music generated live from the data behind each frame. It has three tracks: Melting Rhythm (Arctic sea ice), Rising Pitch (global temperature) and Green Pulse (land vegetation). Warmer temperatures raise the pitch, greener vegetation adds fuller harmonies, and shrinking sea ice thins the rhythm.

This answers the challenge by translating sight into sound. Every sonification is generated in real time using official NASA datasets, so each new frame becomes a new song. Captions and keyboard controls make the experience accessible.

It matters because Earth science is mostly shown through maps and colours, which leaves out blind and low-vision learners and many young or beginner audiences. Sound gives everyone a second way into the same data, making Earth science accessible, engaging and multi-sensory.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
The Earth Jukebox shows an Earth visual frame and plays music generated live from the data behind it. The user opens the web app, picks a track, and presses play. They can drag a timeline to hear change across years, choose a region on the globe, and read a short caption that describes what the sound is doing. Our pipeline has four steps. First, NASA data and Earth Information Center frames are loaded. Second, Python scripts clean the data and reduce each frame to a few numbers per region. Third, a JavaScript sonification engine converts those numbers into pitch, rhythm and harmony in real time. Fourth, the frame and the sound play together. The rules are the same on every track: higher pitch means warmer air, fuller chords mean greener land, and fewer beats mean less sea ice.

What are the benefits?
Blind and low-vision learners, students who learn by listening, and young or beginner audiences can explore Earth science that is usually only shown through maps and colour legends. Teachers get a memorable way to teach climate and Earth systems.

What is the intended impact?
We want Earth science to be open to everyone. When people can hear change, they notice trends faster and feel more connected to the planet. The project can also grow into classroom kits, museum exhibits and a library of Earth songs.

What tools did we use?
HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the app. The Web Audio API for live sound. Canvas for drawing the Earth frame. Python for preparing the data. NASA GIBS/Worldview imagery. NASA datasets: the Earth Information Center, GISS Surface Temperature (GISTEMP), sea-ice data from the NASA DAAC at NSIDC, and MODIS/VIIRS vegetation indices. No special hardware is needed, only a browser. We used Claude (Anthropic) to help draft the text and code. All visuals are drawn by code, and no NASA logos appear in AI content.

How is it creative?
It turns satellite data into music, with one consistent sound language so a listener learns once and understands every track. Notes snap to a pentatonic scale, so any value sounds pleasant. Every note is generated live, with no recordings, so any new frame automatically gets its own song.

What factors did we consider?
Accessibility (keyboard control, screen-reader labels, captions, high contrast), scientific honesty (the mapping is shown to listeners and the data is never exaggerated), safe listening (capped volume and gentle fades), and clear credit to NASA and our AI use.
